claim: Measured on direct-edge questions, language models give high verbalised confidence to most of their false-positive edges, while agreement across prompts is better calibrated, although that advantage is not statistically significant.
quote: cross-prompt and cross-model agreement achieve better mean calibration and discrimination ... not statistically significant after Holm correction
notes: Full title has subtitle 'Evaluating LLMs as Calibrated Direct Causal-Edge Classifiers'; 7 authors, submitted 24 Aug 2026 (v1). 'Much better calibrated' overstates: agreement methods have lower mean ECE/Brier than verbalized and logit-based confidence (Sec 4.2.1), but the paper says the advantage is not significant after Holm adjustment. Abstract also says 80.8% and 84.6% of indirect/reversed false positives receive verbalized confidence >= 80%; logit-based confidence is concentrated near 1.0 regardless of correctness. Cross-model agreement also does better, so the claim could mention it.

claim: Metamorphic testing checks a program without an oracle for each output by checking relations that must hold between the outputs of related inputs.
location: Abstract; Sections 3.3-3.4 (shortest path and Gaussian elimination examples)
quote: The expected output x' of the new input pair (A', b') should be equal to x.
notes: Used the arXiv reprint 2002.12543 (submitted 28 Feb 2020); its front matter reads 'Published as Technical Report HKUST-CS98-01, Department of Computer Science, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, 1998', so both exist and the arXiv copy is the readable record. Abstract: technique 'can be used in the absence of test oracles'. The 1998 report does not yet use the term 'metamorphic relation'; it states expected relations between original and follow-up outputs in worked examples. Claim wording is fine.

claim: A survey of metamorphic testing covers its use across many domains, including machine-learning systems.
quote: the technique has seen successful applications in a variety of domains, ranging from web services to computer graphics
notes: Metadata from Crossref; content read from the White Rose eprint (https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/110335/). Section 5.1.5 'Machine learning' reviews MT for ML applications and supervised classifiers (Murphy et al.; Xie et al.).

claim: CheckList tests NLP models against a matrix of linguistic capabilities and test types, including invariance tests (label-preserving perturbations), and finds critical failures that held-out accuracy hides.
quote: An Invariance test (INV) is when we apply label-preserving perturbations to inputs
bibtex:

  author={Ribeiro, Marco Tulio and Wu, Tongshuang and Guestrin, Carlos and Singh, Sameer},
  booktitle={Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics},
  pages={4902--4912},

  publisher={Association for Computational Linguistics},
  doi={10.18653/v1/2020.acl-main.442},
  url={https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.442/}

notes: Minor correction: in CheckList, invariance (INV) is a test type crossed with capabilities, not itself a capability test; the original wording conflated the two axes. Abstract: held-out accuracy 'often overestimates the performance of NLP models'; CheckList identifies 'critical failures in both commercial and state-of-art models'.

claim: PROV-DM is a W3C data model that records the entities, activities and agents involved in producing a piece of data.
quote: Provenance is information about entities, activities, and people involved in producing a piece of data or thing.
notes: W3C Recommendation dated 30 April 2013; editors Luc Moreau (Southampton) and Paolo Missier (Newcastle), with many listed contributors. Abstract says 'people'; the core structures in Section 2.1 are Entity, Activity and Agent, so 'agents' is accurate. Abstract also: 'PROV-DM is the conceptual data model that forms a basis for the W3C provenance (PROV) family of specifications.'

claim: The Tuebingen cause-effect pairs include DWD climate data (altitude, longitude, temperature, precipitation, sunshine) from German weather stations.
location: Benchmark pair descriptions pair0001-pair0004 (webdav.tuebingen.mpg.de/cause-effect); paper Abstract
quote: DWD data (Deutscher Wetterdienst) data was taken at 349 stations
notes: Title was missing from ref; confirmed above. The paper's Appendix D (per-pair descriptions) could not be read: JMLR, arXiv and ar5iv text extraction all truncated before the appendices. Verified instead from the official benchmark pages that the paper releases (webdav.tuebingen.mpg.de/cause-effect/, which names Mooij et al. 2016 as the citation): pair0001 altitude->temperature, pair0002 altitude->precipitation, pair0003 longitude->temperature, pair0004 altitude->sunshine, all DWD data from 349 stations, 1961-1990 averages. Paper abstract: benchmark of '100 different cause-effect pairs selected from 37 data sets' including meteorology. If the paper must show the DWD detail in its own text, the author should check Appendix D by hand.
